name: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate

lead: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is a retinoic acid ester used in over-the-counter skincare, best known as Granactive Retinoid. People use it for fine lines, dark spots and acne with less irritation than retinol or tretinoin.

Retinoids speed up skin turnover and support collagen, which smooths texture and evens tone. HPR is described as binding retinoid receptors directly rather than needing conversion, which is the explanation given for its lower irritation. Small Italian studies tested HPR gels in acne and Chinese studies tested it in anti-aging serums, mostly in combination formulas.

paras: It is applied as a serum or cream, usually in the evening, and is often chosen by people whose skin does not tolerate retinol. It is commonly paired with a moisturizer and daytime sunscreen. Visible changes in texture and tone generally take weeks to months of regular use.

Trials of HPR-containing products report mild dryness, peeling, redness and burning, in about 15% of participants in one open study. A laboratory study found retinoid products often lose potency with light and storage. Pregnancy safety data for HPR were not found, and retinoids in general are usually avoided during pregnancy.

chain: Fewer fine lines, more even tone
angle.text: HPR, sold as Granactive Retinoid, is a gentler cosmetic retinoid: it acts on skin cells to speed turnover and support collagen, so fine lines soften and dark spots even out. People who find retinol irritating often choose it, and published human studies are small and mostly use combination products.

lead: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is a synthetic retinoid ester used in cosmetic skincare to smooth fine lines, even out the look of photoaged skin and keep acne-prone skin clearer, either on its own or alongside retinol or retinyl propionate.[1][2][3] It is sold as an over-the-counter ingredient rather than a drug, and it is promoted as a retinoid for people whose skin finds retinol or prescription tretinoin too irritating.[4]

Its best-known commercial form is Granactive Retinoid, a trademarked mixture of 10% HPR in dimethyl isosorbide developed by Grant Industries, which Grokipedia dates to late 2014 and says was licensed to consumer brands including The Ordinary.[4] A 2021 stability study treated it as a newer retinoid in commercial cosmetics alongside retinol, retinyl palmitate and beta-carotene.[5]

Sources describe its chemistry slightly differently: a 2015 clinical paper calls it a synthetic ester of 9-cis-retinoic acid, whereas Grokipedia describes it as the pinacolyl ester of all-trans retinoic acid.[1][4] Marketing materials describe it as binding retinoid receptors directly, without needing conversion in the skin, and as less irritating than retinol.[4]
Research on HPR in people consists of small open or comparative studies, most using combination products for acne or photoaging, together with in-vitro and zebrafish work.[1][6][7][2][8][9]
infobox: HPR; Granactive Retinoid (trademarked 10% HPR in dimethyl isosorbide) [4]
Cosmetic ingredient; retinoic acid itself is banned in cosmetics [11]

paras: HPR is incorporated into serums and creams aimed at wrinkles and photoaging, and into gels for mild to moderate acne.[1][2][9] Grokipedia says suppliers recommend using it at roughly 1 to 2 percent of the oil phase of an emulsion, and that the ingredient is also positioned for colour cosmetics and body care.[4]

In consumer skincare, products built on it are positioned as a starting point for people new to retinoids or with sensitive skin, a reading supported by the stated motivation in some Chinese anti-aging work, where skin intolerance with retinoids is cited as the reason for HPR combinations.[2]

Retinoids are the family of vitamin A and its derivatives. Retinol and its esters are not directly active: the skin converts them step by step into retinoic acid, which binds retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and retinoid X receptors that regulate gene activity in skin cells.[10] First-generation retinoids such as tretinoin are retinoic acids themselves, which is part of why prescription tretinoin is potent and also why it irritates.[10]

HPR is an ester of retinoic acid with a pinacolone-derived group. Grokipedia gives its formula as C26H38O3 and says it is stable in oil-based systems, insoluble in water, and about ten times more resistant to thermal oxidation than retinol in a manufacturer test at 50 degrees Celsius, though still sensitive to light.[4] The manufacturer-derived claim that it binds receptors directly rather than via conversion is the stated basis for its lower irritation; the independent trials reviewed here do not compare it head to head with tretinoin.[4]

HPR is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient, not as a drug, and Grokipedia notes it is described as complying with regulations in China.[4] A quality-control study of commercial retinoid cosmetics screened products for retinoic acid, which is prohibited in cosmetics, because retinoid claims on labels cannot be assumed to match contents.[11] Retinoic acid esters and retinoids as a class carry pregnancy warnings in their oral and prescription forms; Wikipedia states that oral retinoids can cause serious birth defects and that topical tretinoin is not recommended in the first trimester, although evidence of harm from topical use is limited.[10] Pregnancy data specific to HPR have not been published.

Acne. In a sponsor-free, open, multicenter pilot study, 98 patients aged 15 to 40 with mild to moderate facial acne used a gel combining 0.1% HPR, 1% retinol in glycospheres and 2% papain once daily for 12 weeks; the authors reported a 41% mean reduction in Global Acne Grading System score and a 40.8% reduction in total lesions, with mild to moderate local effects (dryness, peeling, erythema, burning) in 15.3% and no discontinuations [1]. In a 12-month maintenance study, 40 patients with moderate acne who had achieved remission on oral isotretinoin then used an HPR and retinol glycosphere gel; 6 of 39 completers (15.38%) relapsed and no adverse events were reported [6]. Other small Italian studies tested HPR in mixtures with azelaic acid and alpha-hydroxy acids plus a probiotic (30 patients, 60 days) and with an antimicrobial peptide, salicylic acid, glycolic acid and niacinamide (2-month prospective study) [9][12]. All are uncontrolled or combination studies, so HPR's separate contribution is not isolated.

Skin aging. A 2023 paper combined in-vitro fibroblast work with an in-vivo serum evaluation to test an HPR and retinyl propionate combination for dermal remodeling and irritation, and a 2025 comparative study examined a topical HPR-peptide product against a single fractional CO2 laser treatment over 16 weeks in women with moderate photodamage [2][8]. A comparison of five retinoids, including HPR, evaluated anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative activity in vitro and in vivo for photoaging [7]. A nanoparticle formulation of retinyl propionate and HPR was reported to have high stability and low irritation in a 2023 paper [3].
Laboratory safety work. A zebrafish study of a microencapsulated HPR ingredient assessed irritation and developmental toxicity compared with a reference HPR product [13].
Head-to-head human trials comparing HPR with tretinoin or retinol as single agents were not found in the studies reviewed.

In the acne pilot, 15.3% of patients had mild to moderate dryness, peeling, erythema or burning [1]. Skin intolerance with retinoids in general is cited as the motivation for HPR combinations in anti-aging work, particularly among Chinese users [2]. The zebrafish study reported that an HPR reference product increased an irritation measure at a lower concentration than the microencapsulated ingredient, and calculated teratogenicity indices for both [13].

A 2021 study of 12 commercial cosmetics reported that retinoids degraded over 6 months in almost all products, with declines of 0 to 80% at 25 degrees C and 40 to 100% at 40 degrees C, with light causing more degradation than heat; HPR was among the compounds tested [5]. A separate quality-control study examined labeling and retinoid content in commercial products and screened for retinoic acid, which is prohibited in cosmetics [11].

According to Grokipedia, Grant Industries announced Granactive Retinoid in early 2015 after foundational testing in late 2014, registered the trademark in 2017, and licensed it to consumer brands including The Ordinary, which began featuring it around 2016.[4] The company positioned it as a next-generation, low-irritation alternative to retinol, with in-house patch testing reported to show lower irritation than retinyl palmitate.[4]

Since then HPR has spread through the retinoid segment of skincare, often appearing in serums beside retinol or retinyl propionate, and Chinese cosmetic research groups have published several combination studies on it.[2][8][3] Online skincare communities discuss it as a middle step between retinol and prescription retinoids; the published literature does not rank it against them.
